title: Water is heaviest at 4°C
hook: Water is at its densest a few degrees above freezing, not at 0°C.
peek: Almost every liquid gets denser as it cools. Fresh water stops doing so at about 4°C and starts to expand. That small quirk is why lakes freeze from the top down and stay liquid underneath.
lede: Most liquids shrink steadily as they get colder. Fresh water shrinks only until it reaches about 4°C. Cool it further and it starts to expand again, and when it freezes it grows by about 9%. So the densest water in a lake is not the coldest. It is water at around 4°C, and that water sinks to the bottom.

bullets.text: In autumn, surface water cools, sinks and stirs the lake until all of it reaches about 4°C. After that, colder water stays on top and freezes, and the ice cap insulates the liquid below, which stays near 4°C all winter.

Water molecules cling to each other with hydrogen bonds. As water cools, more of them lock into open, ice-like rings that hold molecules further apart. Below about 4°C that spreading wins over normal shrinking.
Salt changes the rule. Ordinary seawater keeps getting denser all the way down to its freezing point, about minus 2°C, so oceans do not settle into the same layers as freshwater lakes.
French scientists in 1799 defined the kilogram as the mass of a litre of water at its densest, around 4°C. They picked that temperature because a small change either side barely affects the density.
